To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV infection is associated with abnormal expression and function in the DNA sensors IFI16, cGAS and IFI44L, and IFI16 correlates with immune activation and T‐cell depletion.
HIV infection impairs expression and function of innate DNA sensors in PBMC, and expression levels of IFI16 correlate with chronic immune activation and viral load.
HIV infection leads to impaired expression of interferons and IFI16 and that expression of IFI16 correlates with chronic immune‐activation in HIV patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
innate immunity and the role of DNA sensing in HIV infection.
innate immune recognition of HIV and the role of DNA sensing in HIV pathogenesis.
the mechanisms by which the innate immune system is affected by HIV infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the DNA sensors are not impaired in HIV‐positive patients, but rather that the expression and function of IFI16 are altered in the presence of HIV‐1 infection, and may contribute to the chronic immune activation seen in these patients.
the innate immune system has an impact on chronic immune activation and HIV‐associated pathogenesis.
HIV infection is associated with altered DNA sensing and signalling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

HIV‐infected individuals have a dysregulated DNA sensing system, and that the expression of IFI16 is associated with increased T cell activation, which may be a consequence of IFI16‐induced DNA sensing.
DNA‐mediated signalling in the context of HIV infection is impaired and that IFI16 is up‐regulated in HIV patients, correlating with immune activation and low CD4 count.
DNA sensing and signalling is impaired in HIV infection, and that this is associated with a higher viral load and lower CD4 cell count.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the innate immune system is important for HIV infection, and that the DNA sensors are involved in the pathogenesis.
the expression and function of DNA sensing pathways are altered in HIV patients and this may have implications for the pathogenesis of the disease.
HIV infection is associated with impaired expression and function of DNA sensing and signalling, which may have consequences for chronic immune activation and the development of immunosuppression.
